newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Time runs out for Bosnia's econ reforms - Bildt.
newsitem.headline: Time runs out for Bosnia's econ reforms - Bildt.

text.p: Time is running out for the Bosnian government to adopt a set of economic laws if it wants to see more money raised for the country's reconstruction at a donors conference in April, western officials said on Tuesday.

Spokesman for the office of the High Representative in Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said it was concerned that the government's slow pace could further delay the fund-raising conference, already re-scheduled from March until mid-April.

"Without these draft laws adopted and they are the minimum...it will push back any agreement with the International Monetary Fund and that, in turn, will damage the donors conference," Colum Murphy said.

Carl Bildt's office had proposed to the government in January a set of economic reform laws which need to be adopted before the upcoming conference in Brussels. Both the laws and an agreement with IMF are required before the conference.

The set includes a central bank law, budget laws, external debt law and a tariff law. IMF officials say they need to see the central bank functioning and budget laws agreed upon before clinching a deal with the government.

International donors want to see economic changes in Bosnia before they commit more funds for the reconstruction, foreign experts say. An IMF agreement is a standard procedure before a pledging conference.
The nature of foreign assistance in Bosnia has changed from bringing emergency relief in 1996 to building a self-sustainable economy, capable of economic growth once donations cease, they say.
But Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic have been slow in responding to international demands, Murphy said.
"We feel they must move much more quickly and the urgency of the draft laws is to some degree escaping people," he said.
The central bank law, leaning on the country's peace accord envisaging one bank and a single currency, is still unpalatable for nationalists.
Serb officials have so far refused to cave in because it would further diminish their drive for a separate state.

The Serb President Biljana Plavsic recently said that "she would swallow the hard pill of a single currency", but the Serb member of the three-man presidency Momcilo Krajisnik, is yet to agree, a western diplomat said.

A World Bank delegation, currently discussing future financial strategy with officials of both sides, will also press for the solution to outstanding issues when it attends a government's session on Thursday, Murphy said.
